title: You Can Win
author: Shiv Khera
tagline: A step-by-step tool for top achievers — India's best-selling success manual: winners don't do different things, they do things differently.
oneLiner: Success is not an accident: attitude, positive thinking, goal-setting, and character — built step by step, the Indian classic's way.
bigIdea: Khera's blockbuster — one of India's best-selling English books ever — is deliberately old-school: success as CONSTRUCTION, assembled from attitude (the foundation: his famous calculation that attitude, not aptitude, determines altitude), motivation that's internal and renewable (the fire from within versus the flash from outside), self-esteem built through integrity and contribution, interpersonal skills grounded in genuine care, subconscious programming through auto-suggestion, goal-setting with the SMART discipline plus a burning WHY, values and vision as the rudder, and the closing covenant: WINNERS DON'T DO DIFFERENT THINGS — THEY DO THINGS DIFFERENTLY. Stuffed with parables (the elephant's rope, the pond frog, the hot-water frog), action steps after every chapter, and a moral seriousness rare in the genre: for Khera, success without character is failure wearing a costume.
quotes: Winners don't do different things. They do things differently.
Your positive action combined with positive thinking results in success.
Under adverse conditions - some people break down, some break records.

lessons.title: Attitude: The Foundation Everything Sits On
lessons.chapter: Chapters 1–2: Importance of Attitude / Building a Positive Attitude
lessons.summary: Khera's opening claim, backed by his consulting years: study any success and the differentiator is rarely talent, education, or luck — it's ATTITUDE: the settled disposition toward effort, setbacks, other people, and self. His triple-A construction plan: AWARENESS (attitude is caught early — from environment, experiences, education — but remains buildable at any age), the daily builders — focus on the positive (his sorting exercise: the same day contains material for gratitude and grievance; attitude picks the exhibit), make a habit of doing it NOW (procrastination as attitude-decay in action), develop gratitude, continuous learning, build self-esteem through giving, and stay away from negative influences (his 'garbage-truck people' warning predates the viral versions: some people carry loads of negativity looking for places to dump — don't be a landfill). The stakes he sets: attitude compounds bidirectionally — the same slight daily lean, toward constructive or corrosive, arriving years later as character, reputation, and results.
lessons.example: The elephant-rope parable does the chapter's heavy lifting: the adult elephant restrained by a small stake and rope it could snap trivially — because as a BABY the same rope genuinely held it, and the learned 'I can't' outlived the fact by decades; Khera's rooms of executives reliably go quiet at the question 'what's your rope?' The two-frogs pairing completes it: the frog in slowly heated water (gradual negativity, boiled unnoticed) versus the frog dropped in hot water (acute crisis, instant jump) — chronic bad attitude being the deadlier temperature precisely because it never triggers the jump.
lessons.action: Identify your rope: one 'I can't' installed years ago and never re-tested — re-test it this month, at adult strength. Then run the sorter for a week: each evening, list the day's three positives BEFORE any complaint is permitted airtime. And name your garbage trucks; reroute politely.

lessons.title: Motivation From Within: Fireproof Fuel
lessons.summary: Khera's motivation taxonomy: EXTERNAL motivators (fear, incentives, pep talks) work — briefly: fear motivates until the stick leaves the room; incentives until the next raise resets the baseline; rallies until Monday. INTERNAL motivation — pride in work, growth, purpose, responsibility — is the renewable kind, and it's built, not injected: through taking ownership (the motivated employee and the watch-the-clock employee often differ only in whose business they think they're minding), through progress made visible, and through connecting daily tasks to meaning. The SELF-ESTEEM chapters supply the substructure: Khera's definition — the way we feel about ourselves, which broadcasts into everything — is raised not by affirmation cosmetics but by INTEGRITY DEPOSITS: kept promises, honest work when unobserved, giving without scorekeeping (his prescription: 'do something for those who cannot repay you'), and accepting responsibility (the victim posture, however justified, is self-esteem's leading solvent). His caution flags: false esteem from possessions and titles ('borrowed feathers') molts under pressure; the real article survives audit.
lessons.example: Khera's hospital story anchors internal motivation: the janitor asked what his job was — 'I help save lives; if my floors aren't sterile, infections kill patients' — the identical mop drawing meaning or drudgery from the story attached; Khera's point being that the STORY is voluntary, at every desk. The integrity-deposit exhibit is his returned-money vignette: the vendor chasing a customer to return excess payment — 'I was going to find you; I couldn't have slept' — and Khera's audit: the man's esteem account, credited that night, out-earning the note he returned.
lessons.action: Rewrite your job's story: one sentence connecting your daily tasks to the humans they finally serve — posted at the workstation. Bank three integrity deposits this week: one kept micro-promise, one unobserved-quality act, one gift to someone who cannot repay. Watch what the account does.

lessons.title: Goals: The SMART Discipline Plus the Burning WHY
lessons.chapter: Chapters 7–8: Goal Setting / Values and Vision
lessons.summary: Khera's goal doctrine starts with his survey shock: the vast majority drift — not from laziness but from never DECIDING; 'most people don't aim too high and miss — they aim too low and hit.' The construction: goals must be SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, time-bound) but the acronym is the skeleton; the SOUL is the WHY — a reason burning enough to survive the obstacle course (his formula: strong enough reasons make the hows discoverable; weak reasons make every how impossible). The method: write them (unwritten goals are wishes — the writing is the first commitment ceremony), break them into daily bites (the yearly goal has a TODAY component or it's decoration), review at fixed rhythm, and guard the balance wheel: goals across all six spokes — family, health, financial, social, spiritual, career — because a career-only goal-set, achieved, delivers Khera's 'successful failure': the corner office over a collapsed life. VALUES close the loop as the goal-filter: any goal that requires character's discount is repriced as a loss before it's begun.
lessons.example: Khera's air-travel analogy runs the chapter: a flight is off-course most of the time — and lands precisely, because course-correction against a FIXED destination is continuous; the goal-less life corrects against nothing and lands wherever drift delivers it. His balance exhibit is the businessman's deathbed arithmetic — the extra crore weighed against the school plays and anniversaries it purchased-away — Khera's insistence being that the wheel's neglected spokes don't stay quiet forever; they invoice, with interest, at the worst possible hour.
lessons.action: Run the six-spoke audit: one written SMART goal per spoke, each with its burning WHY beneath and its TODAY-bite beside. Install the flight-check: a weekly fifteen-minute course-correction against the written six. And filter every goal through the values gate: what does this cost in character? Reprice accordingly.

lessons.title: Winners Do Things Differently: The Character Close
lessons.chapter: Chapters 9–11: Doing Things Differently / Character / The Winner's Edge
lessons.summary: The closing movement earns the title. Khera's WINNER'S PROFILE, assembled from the book's parables and case studies: winners take responsibility (losers have reasons; winners have results), see opportunity inside difficulty (his line: 'under adverse conditions, some people break down, some break records'), practice persistence past the socially acceptable quitting points, prepare while others wait (luck as the intersection of preparation and opportunity — the prepared, he notes, get 'luckier' every year), and operate from CHARACTER: the chapters on integrity, courtesy, and courage that distinguish this book from its genre — Khera's insistence that a success built on cut corners is a demolition on a timer ('the trouble with the rat race: even if you win, you're still a rat' gets his full Indian-uncle treatment). The final covenant reframes the whole project: winning isn't exotic — the winners' ACTIONS are available to everyone, daily, ordinary; what differs is the doing: consistently, completely, and with the character to deserve the outcome. 'Winners don't do different things; they do things differently' — the book's first line, returned as its verdict.
lessons.example: The persistence gallery Khera assembles is deliberately familiar — the 1,009 rejections before KFC's yes, the failed-at-everything Lincoln timeline, the deaf Edison — but his framing is the addition: at every name he asks 'at which rejection would YOU have stopped?' and lets the room's honest answers grade their own trajectories. The character exhibit is his integrity-under-pressure story: the contractor asked for one compromised beam in an unseen wall — refusing, losing the contract, and being handed, years later, the client's entire portfolio: 'I was testing. Everyone else passed the price test; you passed the character test.'
lessons.action: Take the rejection audit: your last abandoned goal — at which 'no' did you stop, and what does the gallery suggest about that number? Choose one current pursuit and pre-commit to doubling its rejection budget. And run one character test consciously this week: the unseen corner done right, priced as an investment — because per Khera, someone is always, eventually, checking the wall.

lessons.title: The Success Mindset: Winners Do Different Things Differently
lessons.summary: Khera's most quoted line — 'Winners don't do different things, they do things differently' — hides a deep point: success is not about finding a secret activity, it is about transforming how you do ordinary ones. The winner's difference is internal: attitude, discipline, integrity, and the refusal to accept mediocrity as destiny. Khera's framework puts values first: a success built on shortcuts or broken promises is not success but a delayed collapse. The person who combines competence with character becomes the person others trust with opportunity. Winning begins inside, with the daily decision to do the right thing well.
lessons.example: Khera tells of two equally skilled salespeople: one took every shortcut to close deals and one refused to misrepresent the product. The shortcut-taker made more in the short run; the honest one built a reputation that made him the market leader for decades.
lessons.action: Identify one area where you've been taking the 'easier wrong' instead of the 'harder right'. Choose the harder right this week — once, deliberately, and notice how it feels.

lessons.title: Service and Success: The Paradox of the Giving Hand
lessons.summary: Khera's least-discussed but most important chapter: lasting success comes from service — solving others' problems so well that success becomes a by-product. The mindset shift: instead of asking 'how do I get more?', ask 'how do I give more value?' The person who becomes genuinely useful — to customers, colleagues, community — creates a demand for themselves that no amount of self-promotion can match. Service is not altruism for its own sake; it is the most sustainable strategy in existence, because it aligns your growth with others' benefit. The giving hand, in the long run, always receives more than the grasping one.
lessons.example: Khera cites businesses that treat every customer interaction as a service opportunity and grow through referrals alone — while competitors spend fortunes on advertising to win the customers the service-driven businesses keep for free.
lessons.action: This week, do one act of service with no expectation of return — help a colleague, mentor someone junior, solve a customer's problem beyond what's asked.

actionPlan: Snap the rope: re-test one childhood 'I can't' at adult strength.
Rewrite the job story; bank three integrity deposits weekly.
Write six SMART goals with burning WHYs and today-bites; fly the weekly course-check.
Double the rejection budget on one pursuit.
Pass one unseen character test — build the wall right.
caveat: Khera's 'winning attitude' is Indian self-help's foundation — and the Osborne effect is its business shadow: Osborne Computer announced its brilliant next machine with total confidence, and the announcement killed sales of the current one so fast the company collapsed. Winning isn't just believing you'll win; it's understanding what your wins and even your announcements do to the people around you. Confidence must be timed; premature confidence is a self-inflicted loss.
